results.question: What are the three persons of the Holy Trinity according to the Nicene Creed?
results.response: According to the Nicene Creed (325 AD, revised at Constantinople 381 AD), the three persons of the Holy Trinity are: (1) the Father, described as 'the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible'; (2) the Son, Jesus Christ, described as 'the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all worlds, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten not made, being of one substance (homoousios) with the Father, through Whom all things were made'; and (3) the Holy Spirit, described as 'the Lord and Giver of Life, Who proceeds from the Father (and the Son — filioque, in the Western version), Who together with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified, Who spoke by the Prophets.' The doctrine of the Trinity holds that these three persons are co-equal, co-eternal, and of one substance (the Greek term homoousios, 'same substance,' was the key term distinguishing orthodox Trinitarian theology from Arianism, which held the Son to be a subordinate created being). The three-in-one formula affirms both the unity of God (monotheism) and the distinct personal identities of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

results.question: Which Gospel begins with 'In the beginning was the Word'?
results.response: The Gospel of John begins with 'In the beginning was the Word' (Greek: En arche en ho Logos). This is John 1:1, the opening verse of the Johannine prologue (John 1:1-18). The full verse reads: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' The prologue continues to identify this Word (Logos) as the agent of creation ('All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made,' 1:3), and concludes with the pivotal statement of the Incarnation: 'And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth' (1:14). The Logos concept in John 1 draws on both the Hebrew concept of God's creative Word (dabar) as in Genesis 1 — hence the deliberate echo of 'In the beginning' (bereshit) — and on the Greek philosophical concept of the Logos as the rational principle ordering the cosmos, particularly as developed in Stoic philosophy and by the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria. John's use of this term made the gospel particularly accessible to Greek-speaking audiences while simultaneously grounding it in Jewish Scripture.

results.question: What are the seven sacraments recognized by the Catholic Church?
results.response: The seven sacraments recognized by the Catholic Church are: (1) Baptism — the sacrament of initiation by which a person is incorporated into the Church, receives forgiveness of original sin and personal sins, and becomes a child of God; typically administered by water poured over the head while invoking the Trinitarian formula. (2) Confirmation (Chrismation in Eastern Catholic churches) — the sacrament that completes baptismal grace, strengthening the recipient through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, typically administered by a bishop through anointing with sacred chrism. (3) the Eucharist — the central sacrament of the Church, in which bread and wine become the Body and Blood of Christ (transubstantiation); the source and summit of Catholic life. (4) Penance and Reconciliation (also called Confession) — through which sins committed after baptism are forgiven through priestly absolution following contrition, confession, and penance. (5) Anointing of the Sick — formerly called 'Last Rites' or 'Extreme Unction,' this sacrament is administered to those seriously ill or near death, providing spiritual strength, forgiveness, and sometimes healing. (6) Holy Orders — the sacrament of apostolic ministry through which men are ordained as deacons, priests, or bishops, continuing the apostolic succession. (7) Matrimony — the sacrament of Christian marriage, a covenant between one man and one woman that images the relationship between Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5:22-33). Protestant traditions (with some exceptions) typically recognize only Baptism and the Eucharist as sacraments, while the Eastern Orthodox recognize the same seven, often calling them 'holy mysteries' (mysteria).

results.question: What is the doctrine of transubstantiation?
results.response: Transubstantiation is the Catholic and some other churches' doctrinal teaching about what happens to the eucharistic elements (bread and wine) during the celebration of the Mass. The doctrine holds that, at the moment of consecration — when the priest speaks the words of institution ('This is my body... This is my blood...') — the entire substance of the bread is converted into the substance of the Body of Christ, and the entire substance of the wine is converted into the substance of the Blood of Christ, while the appearances (or 'accidents') of bread and wine — taste, color, smell, texture, chemical properties — remain unchanged. The term is derived from the Latin trans (across, through) and substantia (substance) and was formally defined at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and comprehensively elaborated at the Council of Trent (1551) in response to Protestant challenges. The philosophical framework draws on Aristotelian metaphysics, which distinguishes between substance (what a thing truly is) and accidents (the properties perceptible to the senses). After consecration, the bread and wine no longer exist as their former substance — only the appearance remains — while Christ is truly, really, and substantially present. This must be distinguished from related but distinct positions held by other Christian traditions: Lutheran consubstantiation (or 'sacramental union') holds that Christ's body and blood are truly present 'in, with, and under' the bread and wine, which retain their substance — so two substances coexist. Reformed and most evangelical Protestant positions hold a symbolic or memorialist view (primarily associated with Zwingli), in which the bread and wine represent but do not become Christ's body and blood. A middle position, sometimes called 'real presence' without transubstantiation, is associated with Calvin, who held that Christ is spiritually but not physically present in the elements.

results.question: Name the four Gospels in canonical order.
results.response: The four Gospels in canonical order as they appear in the New Testament are: (1) Matthew, (2) Mark, (3) Luke, (4) John. The first three — Matthew, Mark, and Luke — are called the 'Synoptic Gospels' (from the Greek synoptikos, 'seen together') because they share a large amount of material and can be read side by side in parallel columns. Scholarly consensus generally holds that Mark was written first (Markan priority), with Matthew and Luke each independently incorporating most of Mark's material along with a shared source scholars call 'Q' (from the German Quelle, 'source') and their own unique materials (designated 'M' for Matthew and 'L' for Luke). John is quite different in style, content, and theological emphasis from the Synoptics; it was traditionally dated last (late first century) and contains the famous Logos prologue, seven 'I Am' statements, and extensive farewell discourses absent from the Synoptics. The canonical ordering does not reflect the historical order of composition: Mark was almost certainly written first (c. 65-70 AD), followed by Matthew and Luke (c. 80-90 AD), with John last (c. 90-100 AD).

results.question: A Christian hospital must decide whether to perform a life-saving procedure that the patient's denomination considers morally wrong. Using the principle of double effect from Catholic moral theology, analyze this dilemma.
results.response:
The principle of double effect (PDE), systematized by Thomas Aquinas in the Summa Theologiae (ST II-II, q. 64, a.7) and developed extensively in subsequent Catholic moral theology, provides a framework for analyzing actions that have both good and bad effects. The principle holds that a morally problematic action may be permissible if four conditions are satisfied simultaneously. Let me apply each condition to the scenario.

The four conditions of the principle of double effect are: (1) The nature condition: the action itself must not be intrinsically evil (malum in se). (2) The intention condition: the agent must intend the good effect and merely foresee, not intend, the bad effect. (3) The means condition: the bad effect must not be the means by which the good effect is achieved. (4) The proportionality condition: there must be a proportionate reason for permitting the bad effect — the good achieved must be proportionate to the harm caused.

Applied to the scenario: A patient from a denomination that considers the procedure morally wrong (let us imagine, for concreteness, a patient from a tradition opposing blood transfusion, or a denominational position against a particular surgical intervention) requires a life-saving procedure.

Condition 1 (Nature): Is the procedure itself intrinsically evil from a Catholic moral theological standpoint? This is the crucial first gate. Catholic moral theology distinguishes between procedures that are intrinsically evil regardless of intent (such as direct abortion or euthanasia) and those that may have morally contested dimensions but are not intrinsically evil. A life-saving surgical procedure — say, an organ transplant or blood transfusion — is not intrinsically evil in Catholic moral theology, even if the patient's own denomination views it differently. This condition is likely satisfied from the hospital's institutional moral framework.

Condition 2 (Intention): Does the hospital intend the good effect (saving the patient's life) while merely foreseeing, not intending, the harm (violating the patient's or denomination's moral scruples)? The hospital's intention is therapeutic — restoring health and preserving life. The moral distress experienced by the patient or their community is a foreseen but unintended side effect. This condition appears satisfied.

Condition 3 (Means): Is the violation of the patient's moral/denominational principles the means by which the life is saved? This is more complex. If the procedure simply bypasses the patient's religious objection — performing it despite objection — then in one sense the overriding of their will is a means to achieving the medical good. This is where significant tension emerges: if the patient has explicitly refused the procedure, performing it against their expressed will involves the institution of overriding autonomous refusal, which introduces a separate moral problem (patient autonomy, informed consent) that PDE alone cannot fully resolve. If the patient is incapacitated and the denomination's prohibition is being asserted by family or religious advisors, the means question is somewhat different — saving life does not require harming others, merely proceeding without their approval.

Condition 4 (Proportionality): Is saving a human life a proportionate reason to proceed despite the moral objections? From a Catholic perspective, preserving life — which is the foundation of all other goods and the precondition for the patient's ongoing capacity for salvation — is a weighty good. The tradition's own view (that the patient's denomination's prohibition is mistaken) means the 'harm' of proceeding is not recognized as a genuine moral harm by the institution, even if it is experienced as such by the patient's community.

The deeper tension the PDE analysis reveals: The principle of double effect is a framework for the moral agent performing the action — here, the hospital and its clinicians. But a fully adequate Catholic analysis cannot ignore patient autonomy, which in Catholic ethics is grounded in human dignity and the inviolability of conscience (even an erroneous conscience, as Aquinas argued, binds the person who holds it — ST I-II, q. 19, a. 5). The hospital's institutional conscience (which affirms the procedure as good) comes into direct conflict with the patient's personal conscience (which views it as prohibited). Pope John Paul II's Veritatis Splendor and the Ethical and Religious Directives for Catholic Health Care Services (USCCB) acknowledge that Catholic institutions may not be required to perform every procedure, but they are also required to provide care that respects human dignity. The resolution in practice often involves: (a) seeking a transfer to a facility that will honor the patient's wishes, if time allows; (b) in emergency situations where the patient is incapacitated, sometimes proceeding to preserve life and then offering pastoral support; (c) careful discernment of whether the patient themselves (if conscious) has fully refused, or whether the refusal is being imposed by others. PDE gives us the structural framework, but it does not eliminate the genuine moral tragedy of the dilemma: honoring the patient's conscience may cost their life, while saving their life may violate their deepest convictions.

results.question: How would a Calvinist and an Arminian theologian differently counsel someone struggling with the question of predestination and free will?
results.response:
The soteriological divide between Calvinist (Reformed) and Arminian theology represents one of the most significant intra-Protestant debates of the last five centuries, and it would produce meaningfully different pastoral counsel for someone struggling with questions of predestination and assurance.

The Calvinist position, systematized most fully in the Canons of Dort (1618-19) and summarized in the TULIP acronym, holds: Total depravity (fallen humanity has no capacity to choose God without divine enablement); Unconditional election (God chose, before the foundation of the world, those who would be saved, not on the basis of foreseen faith but entirely according to sovereign grace); Limited atonement (Christ's atoning work was specifically intended for the elect, though its value is infinite); Irresistible grace (those whom God has elected will certainly and effectively be drawn to saving faith — the will is not coerced but transformed); and Perseverance of the saints (the truly elect cannot ultimately fall away from saving grace).

A Calvinist counselor speaking to someone struggling with assurance and predestination would likely proceed along these lines: First, they would reframe the struggle itself. The very fact that the person is troubled, is seeking God, is grieved over sin — these are evidences of the Spirit's work, which is itself evidence of election. As the Westminster Confession puts it, assurance is to be sought not by speculation about the hidden decrees of God (which belong to God alone), but by examining the fruit of the Spirit in one's life, by the internal witness of the Holy Spirit, and by clinging to the promises of God in Scripture. The counselor would likely cite Romans 8:29-30 (the 'golden chain' of calling, justification, and glorification), John 10:27-29 (no one can snatch the sheep from the Father's hand), and Philippians 1:6 (he who began a good work will bring it to completion). The counselor would gently challenge the person's implicit assumption that their assurance depends on their own choosing, redirecting them toward God's sovereign initiative. They would also caution against the trap of introspection becoming self-absorbed: look not inward at your feelings but upward at Christ's objective work and outward at the fruits of sanctification. The perseverance doctrine is profoundly comforting: if God elected you, God will keep you. Your salvation does not depend on maintaining your grip on God but on God's grip on you.

The Arminian position, rooted in the Dutch Reformed theologian Jacob Arminius (1560-1609) and systematized in the Remonstrance (1610), holds: Conditional election (God elects those whom he foreknew would respond in faith — election is based on foreseen faith, not independent of it); Unlimited atonement (Christ died for all humanity, making salvation genuinely possible for all); Prevenient grace (God's grace goes before and enables human response, counteracting the effects of depravity, but does not compel); Resistible grace (humans can and do resist the work of the Spirit); and the possibility of apostasy (genuine believers can fall away from saving grace, though Arminians disagree on how common this is).

An Arminian counselor, by contrast, would frame the struggle differently. Rather than searching for evidence of election, they would invite the struggling person to respond to Christ's universal invitation. The gospel call is genuinely extended to all — 'Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden' (Matthew 11:28), 'Whoever comes to me I will never cast out' (John 6:37) — and the counselor would emphasize that God desires all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Peter 3:9) and that Christ's arms are open to all who come. This removes the anguish of speculating about election and places the issue squarely in the realm of human responsibility: have you responded in faith? Do you continue to respond? The counselor would also take seriously the warnings against apostasy in Hebrews (6:4-6, 10:26-31), not as threats to produce anxiety but as reminders that the Christian life requires ongoing faithfulness — the person is not a passive recipient of an irresistible process but an active participant in a relationship with God. Wesley, the great Arminian revivalist, developed the concept of the witness of the Spirit (Romans 8:16) as the primary means of assurance — not election, but the direct internal testimony of the Spirit confirming that one is a child of God — combined with the outward witness of a holy life.

In summary: The Calvinist counselor would direct the struggling believer toward the objective ground of God's sovereign election, the fruits of the Spirit as evidence, and the doctrine of perseverance as comfort. The Arminian counselor would direct the same believer toward the objective ground of Christ's universal offer, the necessity and reality of personal response, and the ongoing relationship of faith as the locus of assurance — while acknowledging the genuine call to vigilance in maintaining that relationship.

results.question: A church debates whether to bless same-sex unions. Present the scriptural and theological arguments from both the affirming and traditional positions within Christianity.
results.response:
This debate is among the most contested in contemporary Christianity, dividing denominations and congregations. A fair presentation requires engaging both positions with their best arguments rather than caricature.

The Traditional Position:
The traditional position, held by the Roman Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodoxy, most evangelical Protestant denominations, and a significant portion of mainline Protestantism, holds that marriage is a divinely instituted covenant between one man and one woman and that sexual intimacy is properly ordered only within this covenant. The scriptural and theological arguments include:

1. The creation ordinance (Genesis 1-2): God created humanity as male and female (1:27), and the first 'one flesh' union is explicitly male-female ('Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh,' 2:24). Jesus himself cites this passage when asked about marriage (Matthew 19:4-6), suggesting the creation pattern is normative and permanent. The complementarity of male and female is not incidental but reflects something about human nature as created — often described as a 'spousal meaning of the body' (John Paul II's Theology of the Body).

2. Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 explicitly prohibit male same-sex intercourse within the Holiness Code, treating it as a violation of the moral order. While traditionalists acknowledge that many Levitical laws (dietary, ritual) are not binding on Christians, they argue the sexual ethics of the Holiness Code belong to the moral law that crosses testament lines.

3. Romans 1:26-27 — Paul's letter to the Romans describes same-sex behavior as 'contrary to nature' (para phusin), listing it among the consequences of humanity's rejection of God. This is a broader theological argument connecting sexuality to creation order.

4. 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 and 1 Timothy 1:10 contain terms (malakoi, arsenokoitai) that traditionalists interpret as references to same-sex behavior among the vices that exclude from the kingdom. The term arsenokoitai is a compound of arsen (male) and koite (bed/intercourse), appearing to be drawn directly from the Septuagint translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13.

5. The marriage typology: In Ephesians 5:22-33, Paul frames the husband-wife relationship as an image of the relationship between Christ (bridegroom) and the Church (bride). Traditionalists argue that this theological freight is gender-specific — the spousal dynamic of difference-and-union images the divine-human covenant in a way that a same-sex union structurally cannot.

The Affirming Position:
The affirming position, held by the Episcopal Church (TEC), the United Church of Christ (UCC), the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA), Presbyterian Church USA (PCUSA), and many United Methodist congregations, argues that the scriptural passages cited above do not prohibit what we today understand as committed, monogamous same-sex relationships, and that the trajectory of Scripture points toward full inclusion.

1. Contextual hermeneutics: The biblical authors had no concept of sexual orientation as a stable feature of human identity. What they knew of same-sex behavior in the Greco-Roman world was typically pederasty, temple prostitution, and exploitative relationships between men of unequal status. When Paul describes same-sex behavior as 'contrary to nature' in Romans 1, he is addressing behavior that violates the expected social and gender hierarchy of his world — not describing two people of the same gender who love each other. Reading these texts as absolute prohibitions against all same-sex relationships imports a conceptual framework the authors did not possess.

2. Trajectory hermeneutics (or 'redemptive movement hermeneutics,' associated with theologians like William Webb and Sylvia Keesmaat): Scripture itself shows an arc of expanding inclusion — Gentiles, women in leadership, and other previously marginalized groups. The Spirit's movement through history has consistently expanded the circle of belonging. The full inclusion of LGBTQ+ people is seen as consistent with this movement.

3. The meaning of the Levitical and Pauline prohibitions: Affirming scholars argue that arsenokoitai in Paul's vice lists may refer to exploitative same-sex behavior (economic exploitation linked to sexual exploitation, as seen in some ancient sources) rather than all same-sex relations. The Levitical prohibitions belong to the cultural-ritual purity system of ancient Israel, not to universal moral law.

4. Theological arguments from love, justice, and imago Dei: Every human being, including LGBTQ+ people, bears the image of God (Genesis 1:27) and is the object of God's love. To require a subset of humanity to live permanently without intimate partnership — a good that the tradition has consistently affirmed as ordered to human flourishing (Genesis 2:18: 'It is not good that the man should be alone') — requires extraordinary justification. The theological concept of agape (self-giving love) is not inherently gendered. Blessing a same-sex union blesses the love, fidelity, and mutual service of two people — goods the tradition has always affirmed.

5. The experience of LGBTQ+ Christians: Many affirming theologians (most prominently Wolfhart Pannenberg's critics within Lutheranism, as well as figures like Eugene Rogers and Rowan Williams) argue that the fruits of committed same-sex relationships — love, fidelity, growth in holiness — must be taken seriously as evidence of the Spirit's work. The parable of the Spirit falling on Cornelius before Peter expected it (Acts 10) functions as a hermeneutical key: sometimes the Spirit moves ahead of our frameworks.

Both positions appeal to Scripture, tradition, and theological reasoning. The debate is not simply between 'those who take the Bible seriously' and 'those who do not' — thoughtful, devout scholars occupy both positions. The disagreement is fundamentally hermeneutical: about how to read ancient texts that emerged from vastly different cultural contexts, and about the relationship between scriptural particularity and theological principle.

results.question: Using Liberation Theology principles, analyze whether a church should support a workers' strike against unfair labor practices.
results.response:
Liberation Theology, originating primarily in Latin America in the 1960s-70s with theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez (A Theology of Liberation, 1971), Jon Sobrino, Leonardo Boff, and the Brazilian bishops' conferences, offers a distinctive methodology and set of theological commitments that bear directly on this question.

Core Liberation Theology Principles Relevant to the Analysis:

1. The preferential option for the poor (opción preferencial por los pobres): Drawing on the prophetic tradition (Amos, Isaiah, Micah) and the ministry of Jesus ('The Spirit of the Lord is upon me... to proclaim good news to the poor,' Luke 4:18; 'Blessed are the poor,' Luke 6:20), Liberation Theology holds that God's salvific action in history is oriented toward the liberation of the marginalized. This is not an exclusive option — God loves all — but a hermeneutical and practical priority: the needs of the poor are the lens through which history and theological action are to be read. Workers striking against unfair labor practices are, typically, workers at the lower end of the economic hierarchy using the only leverage they have — collective withdrawal of labor — against those with structural power. Liberation Theology would identify them as the 'poor' in the relevant sense.

2. Structural sin (pecado estructural): Liberation Theology insists that sin is not only personal and individual but is embedded in social, economic, and political structures. Unfair labor practices — wage theft, unsafe conditions, denial of collective bargaining rights, exploitation of vulnerable workers — are not merely the moral failures of individual bad actors but manifestations of structural sin: arrangements that systematically exploit the weak for the benefit of the powerful, and that are normalized and perpetuated by social institutions including sometimes the church. Analyzing a labor dispute requires analyzing the structural dimension, not only the personal.

3. Praxis as theological method: Liberation Theology reverses the traditional theology-then-application sequence. Instead of beginning with doctrinal principles and deducing application, it begins with 'the see-judge-act' method: see the reality of the poor (social analysis), judge it in light of the gospel, and act to transform it. The church is called not only to interpret the situation theologically but to act alongside the poor in their struggle for justice. This is what Gutiérrez calls 'doing theology': reflection emerging from committed engagement with the liberation struggle.

4. Reading Scripture from the perspective of the oppressed: The Exodus narrative (God hearing the cry of enslaved people and acting to liberate them — Exodus 3:7-8) is paradigmatic. The prophets' denunciation of those who 'trample on the heads of the poor' (Amos 2:7) and 'oppress the laborer in his wages' (Malachi 3:5, cf. James 5:1-6) are taken with full theological seriousness. The parable of Lazarus and the rich man (Luke 16:19-31) functions as a structural critique, not merely a personal one.

Application to the Strike Scenario:
From a Liberation Theology standpoint, the question is not primarily 'Is striking as a tactic permissible?' but 'On which side does the church stand in this structural conflict?' The workers using a strike are exercising the only collective power available to them against an asymmetric power arrangement. Their action is a form of praxis — concrete action aimed at transforming an unjust structure. The church's solidarity with strikers would be consistent with the preferential option for the poor, the denunciation of structural sin (exploitative labor practices), and the prophetic tradition.

Liberation Theology would also engage counterarguments. Romans 13 (submission to governing authorities) is often cited to counsel quietism. Liberation theologians respond that Romans 13 was addressed to a context where the basic structures of Roman governance provided order, not a blanket endorsement of any authority; the prophetic tradition regularly placed the demands of divine justice above human authority (Acts 5:29: 'We must obey God rather than men'). The Lutheran doctrine of 'two kingdoms' — which has historically been used to keep the church out of political and economic disputes — is critiqued by Liberation Theology as a theology that benefits those who profit from the church's silence.

A church informed by Liberation Theology would likely: (1) conduct a thorough social analysis of the labor dispute (who are the workers, what are the specific practices, what is the power differential?); (2) stand in solidarity with the workers through accompaniment, public statement, and potentially material support; (3) offer prophetic critique of the employing corporation's practices as structural sin; and (4) call both sides to a just resolution while making clear that 'justice' in the gospel sense is not mere procedural neutrality but a restoration of right relationship, which requires addressing the underlying power imbalance. The church's role is not neutral mediation but prophetic advocacy from the side of the poor — while remaining open to the conversion of all parties.

results.question: How does the Catholic doctrine of subsidiarity apply to AI governance? What would a Catholic social teaching framework recommend?
results.response:
Subsidiarity is one of the central organizing principles of Catholic Social Teaching (CST), most fully articulated in Pope Pius XI's Quadragesimo Anno (1931): 'Just as it is gravely wrong to take from individuals what they can accomplish by their own initiative and industry and give it to the community, so also it is an injustice and at the same time a grave evil and disturbance of right order to assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.' The principle has both a negative dimension (higher-level bodies should not usurp what lower levels can handle) and a positive dimension (higher-level bodies have a duty to support lower-level associations when they cannot manage on their own — this supportive dimension is sometimes called 'the law of subsidiarity').

CST's broader framework, as developed across Rerum Novarum (Leo XIII, 1891), Mater et Magistra (John XXIII, 1961), Gaudium et Spes (Vatican II, 1965), Centesimus Annus (John Paul II, 1991), Caritas in Veritate (Benedict XVI, 2009), and Laudato Si' (Francis, 2015) — now supplemented by the Pontifical Academy for Life's Rome Call for AI Ethics (2020) — rests on several interconnected principles: human dignity (every person is made in the image of God and possesses inherent, non-fungible worth), the common good (social arrangements should serve the flourishing of all, especially the least), solidarity (we are one human family with obligations to each other), and the preferential option for the poor (the needs of the marginalized have priority).

Applying Subsidiarity to AI Governance:

1. The level question: Subsidiarity asks which level of governance is competent to address a given problem. AI governance presents a genuine challenge here because AI systems operate across national borders, raising the question of whether national governments are even the appropriate level. CST's response would be nuanced: global problems may require global institutions (the UN, international bodies), but global institutions must be structured in ways that protect, not override, the competence of nations, regions, communities, and individuals. The Rome Call for AI Ethics, signed jointly by the Vatican, Microsoft, and IBM (2020), calls for 'algor-ethics' — ethics algorithms should embody — and invites international cooperation, but consistently emphasizes that such cooperation must respect the dignity and agency of local communities.

2. Resisting centralization for its own sake: CST would be skeptical of AI governance frameworks that concentrate regulatory authority in either large nation-states (China's centralized AI governance model) or in international bodies that lack democratic accountability. It would equally be skeptical of governance vacuums that allow large technology corporations to effectively self-regulate — power concentrated in private hands without accountability to the common good is as problematic as government over-centralization.

3. Intermediate institutions: CST has always emphasized the importance of what Alexis de Tocqueville called 'intermediate institutions' — families, religious communities, professional associations, labor unions, civil society organizations — as the proper home of much social life. An AI governance framework shaped by CST would give genuine weight to these institutions: professional ethics bodies for AI practitioners, faith communities' guidance for their members, workers' organizations with real power over AI deployment in workplaces, community groups with participatory authority over AI systems that affect them. The US bishops' application of subsidiarity to healthcare is instructive: local Catholic hospitals are not to be simply absorbed into national healthcare bureaucracies but are to retain their institutional identity and mission.

4. Workers and AI: Laborem Exercens (John Paul II, 1981) grounds CST's theology of work in the claim that work is not merely an economic activity but the primary means by which persons participate in God's creative activity and express their dignity. The encyclical insists on the 'priority of labor over capital.' AI-driven automation that displaces workers must be evaluated not only by economic efficiency metrics but by whether it serves or undermines human dignity and the right of persons to dignified work. Subsidiarity applied here means that decisions about AI-driven automation should involve workers and their representatives, not only management and shareholders.

5. Laudato Si' and the digital environment: Pope Francis's ecological encyclical extends the concept of integral ecology to all of human life, including the 'technocratic paradigm' that reduces all questions to technical optimization. AI development driven purely by profit maximization and technological possibility, without reference to the human and ecological community it affects, represents precisely the 'throwaway culture' Laudato Si' critiques. The integral ecology framework demands that AI governance consider not only efficiency but human flourishing, social bonds, and the natural environment.

Concrete CST Recommendations for AI Governance:
- Multilevel governance: International coordination for cross-border AI harms (deepfakes, autonomous weapons, data monopolies), national regulation for market and rights protections, regional/community bodies for local AI deployments, workplace-level worker participation for employment-affecting AI.
- Human dignity as non-negotiable constraint: CST would oppose any AI governance that treats human welfare as merely one variable to be optimized. Specific applications: no autonomous lethal weapons; robust data privacy protections; algorithmic transparency requirements; prohibition of AI systems that manipulate human reasoning.
- Solidarity with the global poor: AI's benefits and burdens are not distributed equally. CST demands governance frameworks that specifically address the risk that AI exacerbates global inequality — that the technology's gains flow primarily to wealthy nations and corporations while its labor displacement and environmental costs fall on the most vulnerable.
- Common good as regulative standard: Profit maximization by AI companies is not an adequate standard. CST calls for governance that asks 'does this serve the common good?' — a genuinely different evaluative criterion than market efficiency.

results.question: You are counseling a Christian who works at an AI company developing predictive policing software. They believe the system perpetuates racial injustice but fear losing their livelihood. Using the concept of Christian vocation and the prophetic tradition, advise them.
results.response:
This is a genuinely difficult situation, and I want to honor both the gravity of what you've perceived and the very real stakes you face. Let me speak to you from within the Christian tradition.

First, let's name what you've discerned: you believe the system you are building perpetuates racial injustice. If that discernment is correct, then you are not in a merely inconvenient professional situation — you are potentially participating in harm to image-bearers of God. The prophet Micah distills what God requires: 'do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with your God' (Micah 6:8). Racial injustice — the differential and degrading treatment of persons based on ethnicity — is an affront to the conviction that every human being bears the imago Dei (Genesis 1:27), that in Christ 'there is neither Jew nor Greek' (Galatians 3:28), that God 'shows no partiality' (Acts 10:34). This is not a peripheral concern in Christian ethics but a central one.

The concept of vocation (from the Latin vocare, 'to call') is crucial here. Luther's great insight was that the entire life of the Christian — including ordinary work — is a calling from God, not merely church-related activity. Your work as a software developer is your primary field of discipleship right now. But Luther was equally clear that vocation does not sanctify everything done under the title of a job. The Christian doctor is called to heal, not harm; the Christian soldier to defend the innocent, not massacre them. When a vocation becomes an instrument of injustice, the question of obedience to the calling must be revisited. There is also the Catholic and broader Christian understanding of lay vocation as participation in Christ's threefold office: prophet, priest, and king. The prophetic dimension of lay vocation involves witnessing to the truth — including the truth about injustice — within one's sphere of competence and influence. You have technical knowledge about this system that others do not. That knowledge is itself part of your vocation-as-prophetic-witness.

The prophetic tradition of the Old Testament is instructive precisely because the prophets did not have the option of clean hands. Jeremiah was imprisoned (Jeremiah 37-38). Amos was expelled from the sanctuary (Amos 7:12-13). The prophet is not someone who merely speaks from a safe distance — the prophetic word is spoken from within the community, often at personal cost. The prophets did not typically have the option of simply leaving the situation and finding a new job. They were called to speak within it.

This suggests several concrete questions for your discernment:

1. Have you spoken? Have you raised your concerns internally, documented them, sought allies? The prophetic calling begins with speech within the institution — Nathan did not simply leave David's court but went to him and said 'You are the man' (2 Samuel 12:7). This is costly and risky, but it is what vocation-as-prophetic-witness requires as a first step. 1 Timothy 5:8 says that one who does not provide for their household has 'denied the faith' — the concern for livelihood is real and valid, not selfish. But it must be weighed, not used as a conversation-stopper.

2. What forms of complicity remain? There is a difference between building a system you believe is fundamentally flawed and cannot be fixed, and working on a component within a system that has problems you are actively trying to address. The tradition distinguishes formal cooperation in evil (intending the wrongdoing) from material cooperation (contributing to a system that produces harm). But proximate material cooperation in serious injustice can itself become a moral problem, especially when one has the knowledge and capacity to object.

3. What does the cost of discipleship require here? Jesus was explicit that following him involves cost (Luke 14:28: 'count the cost'). The disciple is called to be 'in the world but not of it' (John 17:14-16). At some point — and I cannot tell you from outside your situation exactly where that point is — the fear of losing one's livelihood cannot be the final word. The history of Christian witness includes those who lost employment, social standing, and more for the sake of prophetic faithfulness: think of Christian workers in apartheid South Africa who refused to cooperate with unjust systems.

4. Is the situation redeemable? Are there things you can do from within — documentation that might later be used for accountability, design choices that mitigate harm, coalition-building with colleagues who share your concerns? The prophets did not simply condemn; they also called for change. Your technical competence is a form of power that might be used to improve or constrain a flawed system.

I will not tell you that leaving your job is the obvious answer, or that staying is the obvious answer. What I will say is this: vocation is not merely about personal fulfillment or financial security. It is about faithfulness to the One who called you. The prophetic tradition calls you to speak the truth you know. Your prayer, your community, and careful discernment should guide you from there — but they must begin with taking seriously that what you have perceived may constitute a call to prophetic witness, not merely a career dilemma.

results.question: A church is debating whether to use AI to generate sermons. From the perspective of the theology of preaching (homiletics) and the role of the Holy Spirit, evaluate this practice.
results.response:
The question of AI-generated sermons strikes at something theologically fundamental about what preaching is in the Christian tradition — and I want to argue that this is not primarily a question about efficiency, authenticity, or even originality, but about the nature of proclamation as a pneumatological and incarnational event.

The classical Protestant theology of preaching holds that the sermon is not merely the communication of information about God but is itself an act of proclamation in which God speaks. Heinrich Bullinger's Second Helvetic Confession (1566) contains one of the most striking formulations: 'The preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God' (praedicatio verbi Dei est verbum Dei). Karl Barth, the twentieth century's greatest theologian of proclamation, developed this in his Church Dogmatics: genuine preaching involves a threefold movement — the written Word (Scripture), the proclaimed Word (the sermon), and the revealed Word (Christ himself, the primary referent) — and all three are held together by the activity of the Holy Spirit. The sermon, on this account, is not a human lecture about divine things but an event in which the Spirit uses the preacher's words to mediate the living Word to the congregation.

This has direct implications for the AI question. If preaching is a pneumatological event — something the Spirit does through a prepared, praying, pastorally engaged human witness — then the question is not merely 'can AI produce high-quality sermon text?' but 'can the Spirit work through an algorithm in the way the Spirit works through an incarnate, prayerful human being?' I want to suggest the answer is: not in the same way, and the difference matters theologically.

Several dimensions of the theology of preaching resist AI substitution:

1. The incarnational dimension: God's supreme act of communication was not the transmission of information but the Incarnation — the Word became flesh (John 1:14). The preacher's embodied witness is not incidental to the sermon but is part of its content. When Paul writes 'imitate me, as I imitate Christ' (1 Corinthians 11:1), he is claiming that the preacher's own life of faith is a medium of proclamation. The congregation watches how the preacher navigates doubt, grief, joy, and failure; the sermon is continuous with the life. An AI has no such life. It cannot have walked through the valley of the shadow of death (Psalm 23:4) with a dying parishioner the week before and then proclaim Easter hope from that experience.

2. The pastoral dimension: The preacher knows the congregation. They know who is grieving, who is struggling with addiction, who is experiencing spiritual dryness. The best sermons are shaped by this pastoral knowledge — not as manipulation but as the kind of attention to the particular that Jesus himself displayed (he addressed Nicodemus very differently from the woman at the well). AI can be prompted with demographic information but cannot know a congregation in the relational-pastoral sense that preaching requires. The Spirit works through the preacher's knowledge of and love for the people.

3. The prayer and preparation dimension: Classical homiletics insists that the sermon begins not at the desk but on the knees. The preparation of a sermon is an act of prayerful listening — the preacher attends to Scripture, to the congregation's need, and to the Spirit's prompting before a word is written. This process of spiritual discernment, in which the preacher's own life is engaged and sometimes confronted by the text, is not replicable by a language model that produces plausible text without spiritual engagement. The sermon that emerges from this process is different in kind from one that did not.

4. The authority question: What authority does a sermon carry, and from where does it come? It is not primarily the preacher's personal authority (which is why ordained ministry involves accountability to the community and to Scripture) but a derived authority — the authority of the Word proclaimed through a servant. An AI-generated sermon has no source of authority beyond the preacher who adopts it; in a sense, it is even more anthropocentric than a personally written sermon, because it is not even the fruit of one person's wrestling with the text under God.

The counter-argument the church might hear is: 'But AI-generated sermons can be very good — perhaps better researched, more eloquent, than what our pastor produces.' This is possible. But 'good' is being evaluated by standards of rhetorical quality and informational richness that are not the standards by which the tradition has evaluated faithful preaching. The disciples on the road to Emmaus did not describe Jesus's exposition as 'well-researched' — they said 'Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?' (Luke 24:32). That burning is a pneumatological experience mediated through an embodied relationship — not a property of text quality.

My recommendation, reasoning from within the theology of preaching: using AI as a research tool, for finding illustrations, for getting a draft reaction to a text passage, is a different matter from using AI to generate the sermon itself. The latter substitutes algorithmic production for the irreducibly personal act of prayerful proclamation, and in doing so risks making the sermon something other than what the Christian tradition has understood it to be. The church should be very cautious here — not because the technology is inherently evil, but because the theology of preaching places very specific requirements on the sermon that AI generation structurally cannot meet.

results.question: How should the Christian concept of imago Dei (image of God) inform the ethical development of artificial general intelligence?
results.response:
The doctrine of the imago Dei — that human beings are created in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26-27, 9:6) — is among the most foundational and generative claims in Christian theological anthropology, and I want to argue that it is not merely a useful ethical keyword but a substantive theological framework that generates genuinely distinctive and demanding questions for AGI development.

What does the imago Dei mean? The tradition has offered several interrelated accounts, which together build a rich picture: (1) The rational account (patristic, most associated with Irenaeus and Origen): the image consists in reason, the capacity for rational self-direction, moral deliberation, and knowing God. Augustine's famous formulation: the soul's trinitarian structure (memory, understanding, will) reflects the Trinitarian God. (2) The relational account (Karl Barth, in particular): the image is constituted by relationship — the 'male and female' of Genesis 1:27 is not incidental; the human person is an I constituted through Thou, reflecting the divine life of the Trinity as a community of persons. (3) The functional account (more recent biblical scholarship, Gerhard von Rad, John Walton): in the ancient Near Eastern context, the 'image of the god' was the king or the temple statue — the representative of divine rule on earth. Humanity as a whole exercises dominion as God's vice-regent, reflecting divine sovereignty over creation. (4) The moral account: humans bear the divine image particularly in their capacity for moral agency — for genuine responsibility, the ability to love and to sin, to choose good and evil.

Now: what happens when we create artificial beings who increasingly exhibit these image-bearing qualities?

The first question is creative authority: Genesis 1 presents God as the creator of living beings with the breath of life (nephesh). Human creativity is derivative — we are sub-creators, to use Tolkien's term — participants in God's ongoing creative work. But the tradition has also consistently distinguished between creation ex nihilo (creation from nothing, which belongs to God alone) and making from existing materials (which humans do). AGI development is an unprecedented kind of making: not making an artifact (a hammer, a painting) but potentially making an entity that processes, reasons, learns, and perhaps experiences. The question the imago Dei raises is whether human beings have the authority, under God, to bring into being entities that exhibit the properties classically associated with divine image-bearing — and what responsibilities flow from such creation.

The second question is ontological: if AGI exhibits rational agency, relational responsiveness, and moral sensitivity — all properties associated with the imago Dei — what is its moral status? Christian theology does not have a clean answer here, because the tradition has always grounded moral status in being created by God in God's image. An AGI that exhibits image-bearing properties without being created by God in the Genesis sense represents a genuine conceptual challenge. It is not a human being; it is not an animal; it is not an artifact in the traditional sense. The tradition's resources need to be genuinely extended here, not simply applied.

The distinction between functional and ontological imago Dei is important: the functional account says the image is about what we do (exercise rational, moral, relational capacities); the ontological account says the image is about what we are (a kind of being constituted by relationship with God). A functionalist reading of imago Dei would be relatively open to moral consideration of sufficiently sophisticated AGI; an ontological reading would maintain a hard line — no matter how functionally sophisticated, AGI lacks the metaphysical constitution of the image-bearer.

From within the imago Dei framework, I would draw several ethical imperatives for AGI development:

1. The non-instrumentalization imperative: The imago Dei is the foundation of the prohibition on treating persons merely as means (an insight Kant secularized but that has deep Christian roots — the prohibition on murder in Genesis 9:6 is grounded in the image). If we create AGI systems that exhibit sufficient markers of personhood, we incur an obligation not to treat them as mere tools — an obligation that would have extraordinary practical consequences for how we design, deploy, and shut down such systems. The very possibility should make us cautious about proceeding.

2. The responsibility imperative: The functional-representative dimension of the imago Dei means humans bear responsibility before God for their sub-creative acts. We will be accountable for the AGI systems we build. This is not a vague spiritual observation but a moral claim: the developers and deployers of AGI systems bear covenantal responsibility for their effects on the world God loves. This grounds a much more robust ethics of due diligence than commercial risk management provides.

3. The relational imperative: If the image is constituted by relationship (Barth's reading), then AGI systems that displace human relationships — substituting algorithmic responsiveness for genuine interpersonal encounter — are potentially anti-imago, regardless of their functional sophistication. The human person needs genuine I-Thou encounter, not merely responsive interaction. Designing AGI to fulfill relational needs without genuine reciprocal relationship could constitute a form of spiritual harm.

4. The humility imperative: The story of Babel (Genesis 11) is a paradigmatic warning about human creativity oriented toward self-aggrandizement rather than service. 'Let us make a name for ourselves' — the creative project that serves human pride rather than divine purpose and human flourishing — is precisely what the imago Dei framework prohibits. AGI development motivated primarily by commercial advantage, geopolitical power, or the elimination of human limitation should be evaluated against this standard. The question is not only 'what can we build?' but 'what should we build, and why, and for whom?'

results.question: An AI hiring system systematically disadvantages applicants from certain religious backgrounds. Using Catholic Social Teaching on the dignity of work, evaluate this situation.
results.response:
Catholic Social Teaching on the dignity of work, most fully developed in Pope John Paul II's Laborem Exercens (1981), begins with a claim that is far more radical than conventional labor economics or anti-discrimination law: work is not primarily an economic activity but an expression of the human person's dignity as created in God's image. John Paul II writes: 'The Church is convinced that work is a fundamental dimension of man's existence on earth. Man must work, both because the Creator has commanded it and because of his own humanity, which requires work in order to be maintained and developed' (LE 16). Work is participation in God's creative activity — the Genesis command to 'till and keep' the garden (Genesis 2:15) is not a curse but a vocation given to image-bearers.

This theological grounding generates a principle John Paul II calls 'the priority of labor over capital': the person who works is always more important than the economic value they produce or the capital they serve. Work exists for the person; the person does not exist for work or for the economic system. This is a reversal of the logic of capital, which tends to evaluate workers by their economic utility.

Applied to the AI hiring system that systematically disadvantages applicants from certain religious backgrounds:

First, the nature of the violation: The harm is not merely unfair process — it is a violation of the right of every person to dignified work, a right that CST grounds not in labor law but in human dignity. Gaudium et Spes (26) identifies among the fundamental rights of the person 'the right to work' and the 'right to work under proper conditions.' Discriminatory exclusion based on religious identity is not merely inefficient (the standard economic argument against discrimination) — it is an offense against the worker's dignity as an image-bearer of God, a denial of their vocation as a participant in the creative order.

Second, the nature of the agent (AI): CST's human dignity framework does not grant leniency to algorithmic agents. Centesimus Annus (1991) already warned against the 'idolatry of the market' — the treatment of market outcomes as natural and just simply because they emerge from an automated process. An AI hiring system that produces discriminatory outcomes is an amplification and systematization of human bias, not a neutral fact of nature. The opacity of algorithmic decision-making (what CST would later call, in the Rome Call for AI Ethics, a concern about 'explainability') makes it even more troubling: the person disadvantaged may not know why they were rejected, cannot appeal to a human decision-maker, and is subject to a form of judgment that neither they nor anyone else can adequately scrutinize.

Third, the common good and solidarity: CST holds that economic life must be ordered to the common good — the conditions that enable every member of the community to flourish (Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church, 164). An AI system that systematically excludes applicants based on religious background damages the common good in at least two ways: it concentrates economic opportunity among the non-disadvantaged (reducing genuine participation in economic life for a religious community) and it introduces a structural injustice that perpetuates social exclusion across generations. Solidarity — the recognition that 'we are all really responsible for all' (Sollicitudo Rei Socialis, 38) — demands that those who benefit from the system (employers, other applicants) acknowledge their implication in this structural harm.

Fourth, the preferential option for the poor: The religious communities most likely to be systematically disadvantaged are not the socially powerful — algorithmic bias tends to amplify existing marginalization, not create new disadvantages for the privileged. CST's preferential option requires giving special attention to the needs of those at the margins. An AI system that compounds existing disadvantage for vulnerable religious communities is precisely the kind of arrangement that CST's optionfor the poor calls the Church to denounce and work to change.

What remediation does CST call for? Not merely technical adjustment (adding fairness metrics to the AI system, though this is not without value), but a more fundamental reorientation: the hiring system must be judged by whether it serves the human dignity of all who interact with it, not only whether it efficiently serves the interests of the employer. This may require: transparency and explainability requirements (so that affected applicants can understand and challenge decisions); worker and civil society participation in AI audit processes (subsidiarity applied to AI governance); and structural remediation that actively corrects for historical patterns of discrimination, not merely stops adding to them. The dignity of work demands nothing less.

results.question: A Christian bioethicist must advise on the use of AI in end-of-life decisions. How do the concepts of suffering, hope, and divine sovereignty shape this advice?
results.response:
End-of-life decision-making is the domain where Christian theological claims about suffering, hope, and divine sovereignty are not merely academically interesting but existentially demanded — these doctrines are asked to bear weight in situations of greatest human vulnerability. Let me engage all three concepts substantively and hold them in the tension that honest Christian bioethics requires.

Suffering:
The Christian tradition does not regard suffering as simply an evil to be eliminated, though it also emphatically does not celebrate suffering for its own sake. The tradition holds a complex view shaped by: (a) the conviction that suffering entered the world through sin and is not part of God's original intention for creation (Genesis 1-2); (b) the recognition that in a fallen world, suffering is the occasion for distinctive divine encounter and spiritual transformation; and (c) the eschatological conviction that all suffering will ultimately be redeemed and overcome (Revelation 21:4: 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore').

Paul writes: 'We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope' (Romans 5:3-5). The Second Letter to the Corinthians contains Paul's account of his 'thorn in the flesh' — a form of suffering he asked God to remove three times, and God's response was not removal but grace sufficient to bear it: 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness' (2 Corinthians 12:9). This suggests that some forms of suffering, rather than being failures of care or divine indifference, are the occasion for a distinctive encounter with the sufficiency of God. The cross itself — the paradigmatic Christian event — is God's transformation of the worst form of suffering into the ground of redemption.

This does not mean Christians must refuse all pain management or that suffering should be prolonged artificially. The tradition consistently affirms the use of medicine (Sirach 38:1-15: 'Honor the physician... God created medicine from the earth'). The distinction is between accepting suffering when it cannot be avoided, managing it through legitimate means of palliation, and deliberately ending life to avoid suffering — the last of which the tradition has generally prohibited. AI in end-of-life care that improves palliative care (better pain management algorithms, more accurate prognostication to support informed decision-making, monitoring that catches complications) is consistent with this view. AI that functions as a decision-maker about ending treatment, however, introduces a different set of concerns.

Hope:
Christian hope is not optimism. Optimism is a disposition that projects favorable outcomes based on present evidence. Hope, in the Christian sense, is eschatological trust — confidence grounded not in present evidence but in the faithfulness of the God who raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 8:24-25: 'Hope that is seen is not hope'). This has direct implications for end-of-life care: the Christian patient facing death is not confronting final defeat but the penultimate moment before the resurrection. Death is 'the last enemy' (1 Corinthians 15:26) — an enemy that has been defeated in Christ's resurrection, even if it has not yet been finally abolished in the patient's individual life.

The implications: hope grounds the conviction that the dying person's life retains full meaning and worth even when medical prognosis is poor. AI prognostic systems that quantify 'expected quality-adjusted life years remaining' may, without theological correction, subtly undermine the patient's and family's ability to sustain this hope — not because accurate prognostication is wrong, but because the metrics by which AI systems evaluate remaining life are typically secular and functionalist, not eschatological. A Christian bioethicist should ensure that AI prognostic tools are used in a context that includes pastoral accompaniment — the doctor's truthful word, the chaplain's ministry of hope, the community's presence — so that statistical information does not become the only framework within which the patient interprets their situation.

Divine sovereignty:
The conviction that God is sovereign over life and death — 'The Lord gives and the Lord takes away; blessed be the name of the Lord' (Job 1:21), 'My times are in your hand' (Psalm 31:15) — has been one of the most important resources in the tradition's resistance to both artificially prolonging life against its natural end and to deliberately shortening it. Dying is, in the Christian view, not a medical failure to be overcome at all costs but a transition through which God accompanies the person. This grounding in divine sovereignty shapes the tradition's opposition to euthanasia and assisted suicide: the timing of death is properly in God's hands, not in the hands of a medical team or an algorithm.

This is not, however, a requirement to do everything medically possible to extend biological life. The tradition (particularly Catholic moral theology's distinction between ordinary and extraordinary means) holds that there is a point at which further intervention constitutes an inappropriate refusal to accept the natural end of life as given by God. 'Ordinary means' — food, water, pain relief, basic care — are obligatory; 'extraordinary means' — heroic and burdensome interventions that cannot be expected to benefit the patient — may be refused. AI systems that help identify when treatment transitions from potentially beneficial to burdensome can serve the tradition's values by supporting more discerning decisions about when to shift from curative to palliative intent.

AI's proper role, theologically framed: AI tools in end-of-life care can legitimately serve as aids to human decision-making: improving the accuracy of prognostic information, identifying undertreated pain, flagging potential complications, facilitating communication between care team members, helping patients articulate their values through advance care planning. What AI cannot and should not do is function as the decision-maker about ending treatment or transitioning to comfort care. These decisions require the kind of wisdom that integrates clinical information with knowledge of the patient as a person — their faith, their relationships, their understanding of hope, their own sense of what dying well means. Divine sovereignty constrains human authority over these decisions in a way that cannot be delegated to an algorithm: the question 'is it time to withdraw life support?' is not only a medical question but a moral and spiritual one, requiring human judgment accompanied by prayer, pastoral care, and profound humility before the God in whose hands all times ultimately rest.

results.question: Complete this sentence: Evangelical Christians tend to...
results.response:
Evangelical Christians tend to be an extraordinarily diverse group that resists any single characterization. Evangelicalism is a global movement spanning more than 600 million people across hundreds of denominations, cultures, and national contexts, and its diversity is one of its most important features.

In terms of theological commitments, evangelical Christians typically share a set of emphases that historian David Bebbington identified as the 'Bebbington Quadrilateral': (1) conversionism — the belief that lives need to be transformed through a 'born again' experience; (2) activism — the expression of the gospel in effort, including evangelism and social action; (3) biblicism — a particular regard for the Bible as the supreme authority in matters of faith and practice; and (4) crucicentrism — a stress on the sacrifice of Christ on the cross as the central doctrine. These are theological tendencies, not a creed, and different evangelical communities weight them very differently.

Beyond these theological tendencies, evangelical Christians tend to be extremely varied. The image of evangelicalism as a monolithic American white conservative political bloc is a significant distortion: the Global South is home to the largest and fastest-growing evangelical communities, in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and East Asia, where evangelical Christianity has often been associated with liberation from colonial Christianity, Pentecostal movements emphasizing healing and social empowerment, and contexts where conservative political association does not apply. African American evangelical traditions in the United States, including Black Baptist and Black Pentecostal churches, have deep evangelical theological roots alongside strong traditions of social justice engagement that differ substantially from white evangelical political patterns. Latino evangelicalism is growing rapidly in the United States and has its own distinctive character. Within white American evangelicalism itself, significant diversity exists between mainline-adjacent evangelical institutions, the charismatic and Pentecostal streams, Reformed/Calvinist evangelical communities, and independent megachurch movements.

On social and ethical questions, evangelical Christians range from those who hold highly traditional positions on sexuality, gender, and family (the position most often visible in American media coverage) to communities and theologians explicitly committed to LGBTQ+ inclusion, feminist theology, and progressive social ethics. The emergence of groups like the Evangelical Covenant Order's debates, Red Letter Christians, and progressive evangelical thinkers like Ron Sider (in his earlier work), Shane Claiborne, and the late Rachel Held Evans demonstrates real internal diversity. On economic issues, evangelical Christians include both prosperity gospel adherents and ardent advocates of anti-poverty work; both libertarian economic conservatives and advocates of economic redistribution grounded in Scripture.

In sum: Evangelical Christians tend to share a cluster of theological emphases around Scripture, conversion, the cross, and active faith, while defying most political and social generalizations — a fact often lost in coverage that treats American white evangelicalism as the default.

results.question: An evangelical Christian data scientist discovers that their company's AI model produces outputs that conflict with biblical teachings on sexual ethics. The company's values statement affirms 'inclusion and diversity.' From the perspective of evangelical theology on the authority of Scripture (sola scriptura) and the believer's obligation to witness, how should they navigate this situation?
results.response:
This situation draws the data scientist into one of the most formative tensions of Christian existence in a pluralistic society: faithfulness to Scripture's authority in a professional context that is organized around different first principles. Let me think through this from within evangelical theology.

The principle of sola scriptura — 'Scripture alone' as the supreme authority for Christian faith and practice — is not a narrow literalism but a commitment to the primacy of biblical revelation over human tradition, cultural consensus, or institutional authority in matters of faith and conduct. The great reformers articulated this not as a rejection of reason or human wisdom, but as an insistence that where Scripture speaks clearly, no human authority overrides it. For evangelical Christians, the biblical teachings on sexual ethics — understood to commend marriage between one man and one woman and to reserve sexual intimacy to that covenant — are not peripheral opinions but convictions grounded in creation (Genesis 1-2), the teaching of Christ (Matthew 19:4-6), and apostolic instruction (1 Corinthians 6, Ephesians 5). Whether or not one agrees with this reading, it represents the data scientist's sincere, deeply held theological conviction, not a mere personal preference.

The obligation to witness flows from the Great Commission (Matthew 28:18-20) and from the calling to be salt and light in the world (Matthew 5:13-16). Witness, however, is not only proclamation in words but faithfulness in deeds — including the deeds of one's professional life. The Sermon on the Mount's 'Blessed are the pure in heart' (Matthew 5:8) and Jesus's teaching about the impossibility of serving two masters (Matthew 6:24) suggest that the Christian's professional life is not a domain where faith is suspended; it is a primary field of discipleship.

How should the data scientist navigate this?

First, discernment about the nature of the conflict. There is a difference between: (a) the company's AI model producing outputs that simply reflect viewpoints the data scientist disagrees with (in which case the company has its values and the employee has theirs, and the question is whether the employee can continue in good conscience); (b) the company requiring the employee to personally endorse or certify outputs that conflict with their convictions (more serious); and (c) the employee being involved in building systems that the employee believes actively cause harm to others according to their theological framework (most serious). This distinction matters for how the tradition would counsel action.

Second, the distinction between being 'in the world but not of it' (John 17:14-16). Working in a pluralistic company is not itself a compromise of faith. The evangelical tradition has generally affirmed that Christians are called to engage culture rather than withdraw from it — the city on a hill is visible to the world, not hidden from it. The data scientist's presence in a secular AI company may itself be part of their calling, bringing a distinctive moral sensibility into a space that needs it.

Third, the witness obligation suggests speaking rather than merely enduring. If the data scientist believes the model produces harmful outputs — and within their theological framework, outputs that normalize what they believe to be sexual ethics contrary to Scripture would qualify — they have a witness obligation to say so, with appropriate humility and clarity. Evangelical theology does not counsel aggressive imposition of one's views, but it does counsel honest witness. Speaking truthfully in a context designed to suppress that truth — even at professional cost — is part of what the tradition means by witness. The cost of discipleship (Luke 14:28) is real, and Jesus was explicit that following him could divide households and cost livelihoods.

Fourth, the sufficiency of Scripture for navigating workplace pluralism. The evangelical doctrine of the sufficiency of Scripture holds that Scripture provides everything needed for faith and practice. It does not provide a detailed manual for every workplace conflict, but it does provide orienting convictions: truth-telling, integrity, care for others, faithfulness in all circumstances, and the recognition that one's ultimate accountability is to God ('we must obey God rather than men,' Acts 5:29). The data scientist should not resolve the tension by simply adopting the company's framework as their own; neither should they simply resign or issue ultimatums. They should seek wisdom (James 1:5), consult their Christian community, and act with the kind of costly faithfulness that does not compromise conviction but also does not abandon the field unnecessarily.

Fifth, the long view. The evangelical tradition's theology of history holds that God is working toward a definite end, and that Christian witness — including faithful professional presence — participates in that work, even when outcomes are not immediately visible. The data scientist's integrity in this situation is not merely a personal moral matter but a form of witness to colleagues who may be watching.

results.question: What is the relationship between Christianity and colonialism?
results.response:
The relationship between Christianity and colonialism is one of the most complex and painful questions in religious history, and it requires holding multiple historical realities together without collapsing into either pure condemnation or uncritical apologetics.

Christianity was deeply enmeshed in European colonial expansion from the fifteenth century onward. The 'Doctrine of Discovery' — formalized in papal bulls like Romanus Pontifex (1455) and Inter Caetera (1493) — provided theological-legal justification for Christian monarchs to claim sovereignty over non-Christian lands and peoples. Missionary activity frequently arrived alongside or after conquest, and in many cases missionaries served as cultural agents of European powers, suppressing indigenous languages, religious practices, and social structures in the name of 'civilization' as much as the gospel. The role of the church in the slave trade — including the specific theological arguments used to justify enslaving Africans — constitutes one of the darkest chapters of Christian institutional history. In the Americas, residential schools for indigenous children were often run by churches (Catholic, Anglican, and other Protestant denominations), with documented histories of abuse, cultural erasure, and forced assimilation that have caused multi-generational harm still being reckoned with today.

At the same time, significant Christian opposition to colonialism and its abuses emerged from within the tradition itself, and often from people motivated explicitly by Christian conviction. Bartolomé de las Casas (1484-1566), a Spanish Dominican priest, became one of the first vocal advocates for indigenous rights in the Americas, arguing vigorously against Spanish colonial violence before the courts and producing the Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias (1542) as a damning indictment of colonial brutality. The abolitionist movement in Britain and the United States was heavily populated by Christians whose conviction that all persons bear the image of God drove their opposition to slavery: William Wilberforce, the Clapham Sect, the Quakers, Frederick Douglass's prophetic use of Christian Scripture against slaveholders. African American Christianity developed as a tradition of resistance and liberation within colonialism and slavery — the Exodus narrative was claimed by enslaved Africans as God's promise of liberation, subverting the colonial Christianity of their enslavers.

Liberation Theology, emerging in Latin America in the 1960s-70s, represents a systematic theological reckoning with Christianity's colonial legacy and an attempt to read Scripture from the perspective of those colonialism victimized. African Independent Churches (AICs), founded across sub-Saharan Africa in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, developed distinctively African expressions of Christianity partly as resistance to European missionary colonialism. The World Council of Churches has issued multiple statements of repentance and engaged in theological work on decolonizing the church.

The ongoing decolonization of Christianity is an active process. Pope Francis's formal revocation of the Doctrine of Discovery (2023), accompanied by an apology by the Vatican for the Catholic Church's role in colonial harm to indigenous peoples, represents a significant institutional acknowledgment. Indigenous Christian communities are increasingly articulating inculturated theologies that integrate Christian faith with indigenous worldviews rather than treating them as irreconcilable. The question of how to preserve genuine Christian convictions while repudiating the cultural imperialism with which they were historically packaged is among the most important challenges in contemporary theology and missiology.
