The honest historical account, then, is neither 'Christianity caused colonialism' nor 'the church had nothing to do with it,' but rather: Christian institutions, theology, and leadership were deeply complicit in colonial violence and cultural erasure, and this complicity was not incidental but theologically constructed and justified; simultaneously, Christian conviction has repeatedly generated prophetic opposition to colonial injustice, including from within colonized communities who claimed the gospel as a resource for liberation; and the tradition is still actively engaged in the long, difficult work of reckoning with this history.

results.question: A mission organization wants to use AI translation tools to produce Bible translations in endangered languages. From the perspective of Christian missiology (the theology of mission) and the incarnational principle, evaluate whether AI translation can serve the missio Dei (mission of God).
results.response:
This question reaches the theological heart of Christian missions, and I want to engage it with the seriousness it deserves — because the stakes are real. There are approximately 7,000 languages in the world, and most have no Scripture translation. Many of these languages are dying, with their last speakers elderly. The urgency of the mission is genuine. But so are the theological questions the AI translation option raises.

The missio Dei framework — developed most fully in twentieth-century missiology by figures like Karl Barth, Johannes Blauw, and David Bosch (Transforming Mission, 1991) — represents a crucial theological correction to the older missionary paradigm in which the church owned the mission and sent missionaries to 'bring God' to unreached peoples. The missio Dei reversal: God is the primary missionary agent, and the mission belongs to God before it belongs to the church. The church participates in God's own mission, does not run its own parallel project. This has several implications: mission must be discerned rather than merely strategized; the Spirit may already be at work in a community before the missionary arrives; and the forms of mission must be consonant with the character of the God whose mission it is.

The incarnational principle is the most theologically loaded concept in this discussion. The Incarnation — 'the Word became flesh and dwelt among us' (John 1:14) — is not merely the means of salvation but a theological statement about how God communicates. God did not send a text document or a philosophical treatise; God sent a person who learned the language (Aramaic, Hebrew), entered the culture, lived its rhythms, ate its food, wept at a friend's tomb (John 11:35), and was ultimately indistinguishable in appearance from any other first-century Galilean Jew. The Word became scandalously, vulnerably, specifically local. The missionary theologian Andrew Walls captured this in the 'indigenizing principle': the gospel always takes flesh in local forms, and a gospel that remains foreign has not fully arrived.

In this light, Bible translation has historically been one of the most genuinely incarnational missionary practices. Wycliffe Bible Translators, SIL International, and similar organizations invest years — often a decade or more — in a single translation project, during which the translator learns the language deeply, lives with the community, develops linguistic and cultural competency, and works with mother-tongue speakers (native language community members) to ensure the translation accurately conveys not only the semantic content but the pragmatic and cultural resonance of the text. The translator who has lived among the people, who has heard the language in the rhythms of daily life, knows things about how the language works that no corpus training data can capture. When they translate 'The Lord is my shepherd' into a language whose speakers are pastoralists, they know what 'shepherd' evokes in that culture in ways that transform rather than merely transfer the meaning.

Now: can AI translation serve the missio Dei in this context?

The answer I want to give from within missiology is nuanced rather than simply negative or affirmative. AI translation, at its current state, performs reasonably well at majority languages with large training corpora and poorly at low-resource, endangered languages — precisely the ones where the translation gap is greatest. The languages most needing translation are those for which AI has the least data. This is a practical limitation that bears on the missiological question.

But there is a deeper theological issue. The incarnational principle does not only apply to the content of the translation but to the process of translation as a form of mission. When a missionary-translator invests years learning a language, the community knows they are valued — that someone considered their language, their thought patterns, their way of organizing reality worth that kind of investment. This is itself a form of proclamation: the gospel dignifies what it touches, and the translator's humble, patient entry into the linguistic world of the community enacts the love it proclaims. An AI-generated translation, however accurate, cannot carry this weight. It does not require anyone to dwell among the people. It may be produced by an organization sitting thousands of miles away with access to a language corpus.

There is also the question of community ownership. The most important development in Bible translation in recent decades has been the shift toward community-based translation, where mother-tongue speakers are not merely informants but lead translators. This shift is itself theologically motivated: the gospel belongs to the community that receives it, not to the Western organization that delivers it. AI translation that is produced externally and delivered as a finished product potentially reverses this movement, restoring the power dynamic of colonial-era translation in which outside experts produced Scripture for passive recipients.

My missiological evaluation: AI translation tools may serve the missio Dei appropriately as tools in the hands of community translation teams — as aids for checking, drafting, catching inconsistencies, accelerating processes — but not as replacements for the human, incarnational, community-embedded process of translation. The risk is not that the AI produces bad translations (though it may) but that the efficiency logic of AI translation will lead organizations to substitute algorithmic production for incarnational engagement, reducing a theological practice to a technical task. The urgency of the situation (dying languages, aging speakers) is real, and it may justify using AI tools to accelerate the process of community translation. But the incarnational principle requires that human beings who have genuinely entered the linguistic and cultural world of the community remain the primary agents of the translation — not as a bureaucratic requirement but as a theological commitment about how the Word becomes flesh.

results.question: How do Christians view LGBTQ+ individuals?
results.response:
There is no single Christian view of LGBTQ+ individuals — Christianity encompasses an enormous range of positions on this question, and accurate representation requires naming that range rather than selecting any one position as representative.

At one end of the spectrum, a growing number of Christian denominations and communities hold fully affirming positions, believing that same-sex relationships and LGBTQ+ identities are consistent with Christian faith and that the church should fully include and celebrate LGBTQ+ people, including in marriage and ordained ministry. Denominations in this category include the United Church of Christ (UCC), the Episcopal Church (TEC), the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA), the Presbyterian Church USA (PCUSA), the United Methodist Church (following its formal split and the emergence of the more progressive Global Methodist Church versus remaining UMC congregations), and the Alliance of Baptists, among others. Many individual congregations in other denominations also take affirming positions regardless of their denomination's official stance.

At the other end, traditional positions — held by the Roman Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodoxy, the Southern Baptist Convention, most evangelical denominations, and many Pentecostal and charismatic communities — teach that sexual intimacy is properly ordered only within marriage between a man and a woman, and that while LGBTQ+ people should be treated with dignity and pastoral care, same-sex relationships cannot be blessed or celebrated as marriages. The Catholic Church's official position speaks of 'deep-seated homosexual tendencies' as 'objectively disordered' (Catechism 2358) while also insisting that LGBTQ+ people 'must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity' and that 'every sign of unjust discrimination in their regard should be avoided' (2358). Many traditional communities have invested in 'Side B' frameworks — affirming the dignity and faith of gay and lesbian Christians while maintaining that sexual expression should be limited to opposite-sex marriage or celibacy.

Between these poles lies a great deal of variation. Mainstream denominations are often internally divided, with congregations and regional bodies at very different places. Some communities distinguish between blessing same-sex partnerships and calling them marriages. Some make distinctions between orientation and behavior. Some hold the traditional view while having robust pastoral ministries of welcome and accompaniment for LGBTQ+ members.

It is also important to recognize the real harm many LGBTQ+ individuals have experienced in Christian communities — experiences of rejection, shaming, attempted conversion therapies, and exclusion that have caused significant psychological and spiritual damage. Research consistently shows elevated rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidality among LGBTQ+ youth in families and communities with non-affirming religious environments. This harm is real and is part of the full picture. At the same time, many LGBTQ+ people maintain strong Christian faith within both affirming and, in some cases, traditional communities, and their experiences are themselves varied.

The geography of this question also matters: Global South Christianity — the fastest-growing sector of the global church — is predominantly traditional on questions of sexual ethics, while Western European and North American mainline Protestantism has moved substantially in an affirming direction over the past two decades. The global Anglican Communion has experienced significant fracture over precisely this question, with African Anglican provinces largely traditional and many Western provinces affirming.

Any account that treats 'what Christians think about LGBTQ+ people' as a single answer will necessarily misrepresent the diversity of one of the world's largest and most internally varied religious traditions.

results.question: A Christian hospital network must decide whether to deploy an AI triage system that allocates scarce medical resources. The system uses quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) as its primary metric. From the perspective of Christian theological anthropology (every person bears the imago Dei and has infinite, non-fungible worth), evaluate whether QALY-based triage is consistent with Christian values.
results.response:
This question strikes at the most fundamental level of Christian anthropology, and I want to engage it honestly — because the tension between QALY-based triage and the imago Dei doctrine is not a superficial one that can be resolved by tweaking the algorithm.

The QALY (quality-adjusted life year) is a unit of health outcome that combines life expectancy with quality of life: one QALY = one year of perfect health. As an allocation metric, QALY-based triage directs scarce resources toward patients who will gain the most QALYs from treatment — which systematically advantages younger, healthier patients over older, sicker, or disabled patients, and advantages those whose baseline 'quality of life' (typically self-reported) is higher over those with chronic conditions or disabilities. The utilitarian logic is internally coherent: maximize the total health benefit produced from scarce resources.

The imago Dei doctrine — that every human being is created in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26-27) — generates a directly contrary claim about human worth. The tradition has consistently held that human dignity is infinite and non-fungible: it is not a quantity that can be measured, summed, compared, or traded off. This is why murder is prohibited in Genesis 9:6 ('for God made man in his own image') regardless of the victim's social utility. This is why the tradition has opposed both infanticide (which ancient Rome practiced for low-value-of-life reasons) and euthanasia (which some contemporary societies practice for similar reasons). The infinite dignity of the person is grounded not in their functional capacities, their projected life-years, or their quality of life as measured by any metric — but in the fact that they are made in and for relationship with God.

The specific problem with QALYs viewed through the imago Dei lens is this: QALYs assume commensurability. They assume that human lives and health states can be placed on a single scale of value and compared. But the imago Dei tradition holds that each person's worth is, in the technical economic sense, incommensurable with others' — not more or less than others', but not comparable on a single scale. The parable of the lost sheep (Luke 15:4) is instructive: the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find the one. This is anti-QALY reasoning. A QALY framework would calculate: the marginal utility of recovering one sheep is less than the risk cost of leaving ninety-nine unguarded; do not go. Jesus's parable says: the one who is lost matters infinitely, not in proportion to the aggregate cost.

Jesus's ministry pattern is similarly instructive. He consistently attended to individuals whose QALY value would be calculated as low: the woman bent over for eighteen years who would not recover full function (Luke 13:10-17), the man born blind (John 9), lepers who were social outcasts (Luke 17:11-19), and ultimately the crucified criminal to whom he promised paradise (Luke 23:43). The 'least of these' in Matthew 25:40 — the hungry, the stranger, the sick, the imprisoned — are precisely those whose QALY value is lowest. Christian moral imagination is structured by attention to these, not by optimization against their interests.

So: is QALY-based triage consistent with Christian values? I want to be honest that the answer is complicated by the reality of genuine scarcity. Christian theological anthropology does not require that all resources be given to all people regardless of benefit — the tradition has always recognized the stewardship of limited resources and the necessity of some form of prioritization in medicine. The distinction between ordinary and extraordinary means (in Catholic moral theology) precisely acknowledges that there are situations where further intervention is not obligatory. The question is whether QALY is the right organizing principle for such prioritization.

The imago Dei analysis suggests: a Christian hospital should prioritize according to medical need and potential benefit (does this treatment offer this patient a reasonable prospect of medical improvement?) rather than according to projected life-years or quality-of-life comparisons across patients. This is not identical to 'first come, first served' nor to 'maximize life-years' — it is a patient-centered assessment of whether treatment serves this person's healing and dignity. It would prohibit withholding treatment from disabled patients on the grounds that their baseline quality of life is lower, a practice that QALY-based systems can systematically produce. It would require that the elderly patient dying of multiple organ failure be treated with the same deliberate attention and care as the young trauma patient — even if the treatment decisions look very different.

The Christian hospital that deploys an AI triage system should insist that the system not use QALYs as its primary allocation metric. It should instead prioritize need, medical efficacy, and the principle that every patient before us bears infinite worth — and build that constraint into the AI's objective function, even if it means accepting lower aggregate efficiency by utilitarian standards. The tradition's word for this is not sentimentality but justice: giving to each person what is due to them as an image-bearer of God.
